overview.title: 📖 Overview: Real Blemishes, Temporary Ones, and Animals Barred Outright
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 41a–41b
overview.hebrewSource: וְאֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין שׁוֹחֲטִין עֲלֵיהֶן, לֹא בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ וְלֹא בַּמְּדִינָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A summarizing mishna confirms that every blemish taught in the preceding chapter — including the disputed opinions of Ila and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus — is accepted halakha, permitting both slaughter of a firstborn and redemption of other disqualified consecrated animals. The Gemara then turns to the opposite list: conditions that do NOT count as blemishes at all, like temporary pale spots, certain boils, old age, sickness, and foul odor, alongside animals disqualified from the altar entirely because of a transgression involving them. The daf closes with the complex case of a tumtum (indeterminate sex) and an androginos (both sexes) — animals whose firstborn status itself is thrown into question.

slides.title: 🚫 New Mishna: Not Real Blemishes
slides.subtitle: These conditions permit slaughter neither in the Temple nor anywhere else — the animal simply isn't fit at all
headers: Why it doesn't count as a permitting blemish
rows: Pale spots / tears not yet constant
Too temporary — hasn't met the duration test (daf 38)
Internal gums damaged but not extracted
Disqualifies from the altar, but isn't a 'blemish' triggering outside slaughter
Used in a transgression, or killed a person (1 witness/owner's word)
Disqualified from the altar by the Torah's own terms, unrelated to physical blemish

callout.label: Why repeat the permitting list?
callout.text: The Gemara explains the earlier summarizing mishna was needed specifically to confirm the DISPUTED opinions (Ila's additions, R' Ḥanina ben Antigonus) as accepted halakha, not just the unanimous ones.

slides.title: 🩹 Garav and Ḥazazit: Three Kinds of Boils
slides.hebrewSource: גָּרָב — זֶה הַחֶרֶס, יַלֶּפֶת — זוֹ חֲזָזִית הַמִּצְרִית
slides.label: Resolving an apparent contradiction:
slides.text: The Torah itself lists garav and yalefet (ḥazazit) among disqualifying blemishes (Leviticus 22:22) — so why does the mishna say they DON'T permit outside slaughter? The Gemara distinguishes three types: (1) the Torah's garav — dry inside and out, incurable, a true blemish; (2) the mishna's garav — moist inside and out, curable, not a permanent blemish; (3) the garav of Egypt (Exodus 9:10) — dry inside, moist outside, also incurable. Similarly, ḥazazit in the Torah refers specifically to the Egyptian plague-boil; the mishna's ḥazazit is an ordinary, curable boil.

slides.title: 🐂 Disqualified From the Altar by the Word 'From'
slides.subtitle: Leviticus repeats 'min' (from) to exclude several categories entirely — not because of a physical blemish
rows: Won't become young again — needed lest one think only illness disqualifies
Could recover — needed lest one think only permanent conditions disqualify
Not weak, just repulsive — needed as a separate exclusion
Though liable to be killed by court, this teaches disqualification even absent two witnesses
Animal worshipped as, or set aside for, idolatry; one that gored a person to death
Same principle — disqualified on testimony of even one witness or the owner

callout.label: Why the repetition matters:
callout.text: Each case needs its own exclusion because none can be logically derived from another — a sick animal might recover, an old one is merely natural, a smelly one isn't necessarily weak.

slides.title: ⚥ Is a Hermaphrodite's Extra Organ a Blemish?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon vs. the Rabbis — and a deeper question about whether 'cracked' applies to flesh

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: One may not slaughter a tumtum or androginos (hermaphrodite) anywhere — Rabbi Shimon dissents: 'You have no greater blemish than that!' The Rabbis: it isn't even a firstborn at all — just a regular animal.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Why not treat the female organ as a 'crack' (חָרוּץ), a Torah-listed blemish (Lev. 22:22)?

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: 'Cracked' is grouped with 'broken' — just as a break requires a BONE, so does a crack. The female organ isn't near bone, so it doesn't count.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Even without that comparison: since garav (a fleshy boil) needed its own verse to be EXCLUDED, that proves a crack in mere flesh (which would otherwise seem worse) is NOT a blemish on its own.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yishmael
lines.text: Rejects both — I hold a visible crack, even in flesh, counts as 'an ill blemish' (Deut. 15:21).

callout.label: Halakha:
callout.text: The Rabbis' view prevails — a hermaphrodite has no firstborn status at all, so the question of its 'blemish' is moot.

slides.title: 🤔 Was Rabbi Yishmael Even Certain?
slides.subtitle: Rava probes what Rabbi Yishmael actually meant — with real practical stakes

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rava's dilemma: did Rabbi Yishmael mean 'it's definitely a firstborn male, with its blemish,' or merely 'IF it's a firstborn, then it comes with its blemish' — leaving the sex itself uncertain?
2️⃣ Practical difference: if definitely a firstborn, one is flogged for shearing or working it; if merely uncertain, no flogging applies
3️⃣ Gemara tries to prove certainty from Rabbi Ilai's report ('a hermaphrodite IS a firstborn, with its blemish') — but this too could be read as conditional

4️⃣ Rav Ḥisda's distinction: the dispute is only about an androginos (definitely a mixed, separate category, per the Rabbis); a tumtum, by contrast, is agreed by all to be a genuine doubt — definitely male OR female — and therefore consecrated 'due to the doubt' itself

callout.label: Rava's challenge to Rav Ḥisda:
callout.text: If a tumtum is a certain doubt between two fixed categories, shouldn't its valuation (in vows) simply follow whichever value applies? The question is left for further analysis.

summary.principle: Not every physical irregularity is a true, permitting blemish — temporary conditions, curable boils, and disqualifications rooted in the Torah's own exclusions (old age, sickness, transgression) are all distinguished from genuine blemishes, and an animal of uncertain or mixed sex raises the question in its most extreme form.

flowSteps.content: 📋 A summarizing mishna confirms even the disputed blemish-opinions as accepted halakha
🚫 Temporary spots, curable boils, old age, sickness, and foul odor are NOT permitting blemishes
🩹 Garav and ḥazazit in the Torah refer to incurable forms; the mishna's versions are curable

columns.content: 🐂 Animals tied to transgression are excluded from the altar by the Torah's own terms
⚥ A hermaphrodite is ruled to have no firstborn status at all, per the Rabbis

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only genuine, permanent, exposed physical defects count as blemishes — everything else is either curable, or excluded from sanctity by an entirely separate Torah category

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara need to explain that the Torah's 'garav' differs from the mishna's 'garav'?
o: Because the Torah never mentions garav
The Torah's garav is dry and incurable (a true blemish), while the mishna's garav is moist and curable (not a permitting blemish) — resolving an apparent contradiction
Because garav only applies to hermaphrodites
There is no difference; the terms are identical
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes dry, incurable garav (the Torah's blemish) from moist, curable garav (the mishna's non-blemish), resolving the apparent contradiction between the sources.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, why does the Torah use the word 'min' (from) three separate times regarding a sacrificial animal's fitness?
o: It is a stylistic repetition with no legal meaning
To exclude, respectively, an old animal, a sick animal, and a foul-smelling animal — each needing its own exclusion since none can be logically derived from the others
To exclude only male animals
To include additional species of animals
quiz.e: Each exclusion is independently necessary: an old animal is naturally aged (not sick), a sick animal could recover (unlike old age), and a foul-smelling animal is neither weak nor incurable, so none could be inferred from the others.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, why doesn't the hermaphrodite's female sex organ count as the Torah's blemish of 'cracked' (charutz)?
o: Because charutz applies only to the eyes
Because 'cracked' is grouped with 'broken' in the verse, and just as 'broken' requires a bone, so does 'cracked' — and the female organ isn't located near bone
Because hermaphrodites cannot have any blemishes
Because the Torah never mentions charutz
quiz.e: Abaye reads 'cracked' (חָרוּץ) as parallel to 'broken' (שָׁבוּר) in the same verse, requiring the blemish to be at a bone — which excludes the fleshy female organ.

quiz.q: According to the Rabbis' view in the mishna (as opposed to Rabbi Shimon), what is the halakhic status of a hermaphrodite (androginos) firstborn?
o: It is definitely a firstborn with a permanent blemish
It has no firstborn status at all; it is treated as a regular, non-sacred animal that may be sheared and worked
It must always be sacrificed on the altar
Its status depends on which parent it resembles
quiz.e: The Rabbis hold that a hermaphrodite is a distinct category altogether, lacking firstborn sanctity, and may therefore be treated like any ordinary animal.

quiz.q: According to Rav Ḥisda, what is the key difference between a tumtum and an androginos regarding their status as a possible firstborn?
o: There is no difference between them

The dispute in the mishna applies only to an androginos (a distinct category per the Rabbis); a tumtum is universally agreed to be a genuine doubt between male and female, and is consecrated due to that doubt
A tumtum is always female and an androginos is always male
Both are always treated as definitely male
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda distinguishes: the Rabbis' dispute with Rabbi Shimon concerns only the androginos; everyone agrees a tumtum is genuinely uncertain (definitely one sex or the other, just unknown which), and so it is held consecrated due to the doubt.
